text: I’ll model each meridional radius as the single smooth quadratic interpolant through the three specified stations. The outer profile reduces to a straight taper; the core profile remains a smooth quadratic. I’ll revolve the closed annular profile about the engine axis, preserve the four generating edges as the four named patches, and use a coarse unstructured volume mesh first.

The API supports interpolating splines directly. I’ll now create the revolved fluid solid in metres, measure the radii at all requested stations from the defining curves, and render the coarse tessellation before creating any mesh.

The visual check shows the intended converging annulus, with the core swelling near mid-duct and then contracting. I’ll export the CAD solid as STEP, import that exact solid into Gmsh, and inspect its four topological faces so the patch mapping is based on face type and generating-surface geometry—not mesh bounding-box guesses.

The imported CAD has exactly four faces: two planes and two surfaces of revolution. The larger revolved face is the outer cowl, the smaller is the core cowl; the two planar generating faces are the fan exit and nozzle. I’ll now generate only the coarse boundary triangulation and write each named face to its own STL in `constant/triSurface`, before generating the volume mesh.

The four pre-mesh STL files now exist and share the same Gmsh boundary nodes. I’ll fill that triangulated shell with the coarsest practical tetrahedral volume mesh, export Gmsh 2.2 format for reliable patch-name conversion, and convert it to OpenFOAM.

The coarse volume contains 8,808 tetrahedra and all four physical names converted to OpenFOAM patches. The converter’s “undefined faces” message refers to internal faces during reconstruction; I’ll now run the binding `checkMesh`, inspect patch sizes/types, and render the actual OpenFOAM volume mesh boundary for verification.

`checkMesh -allGeometry` requires empty numerical dictionaries even though no solver will be run. The mesh itself is present and the boundary file confirms exactly four nonempty patches. I’ll add only the minimal dictionaries needed by the checker, then rerun it.

The checker expects the standard scheme subdictionaries despite doing no discretization. I’ll provide complete inert defaults (still no fields or boundary conditions) and rerun the same exhaustive checks.

The exhaustive checker passes topology, closure, volume, non-orthogonality, skewness, and connectivity. Its optional determinant test flags 160 boundary-adjacent tetrahedra with only two internal faces—a known diagnostic limitation for tetrahedral boundary cells—while the utility still exits successfully. I’ll also run the standard binding check, which is the relevant acceptance criterion, and directly verify that every requested station point lies on its CAD curve.

The standard OpenFOAM check reports `Mesh OK`. Direct CAD residuals at all six specified radius stations are at numerical zero. The mesh uses metres throughout; no unit conversion is deferred to OpenFOAM.

One caveat: the optional `-allGeometry` determinant diagnostic marked 160 tetrahedra adjacent to boundaries because they have only two internal faces. All standard binding checks pass, and the exhaustive run separately passed closure, topology, positive volume, non-orthogonality, skewness, and connectivity.
